patient.chief_complaint: Since a brain haemorrhage three months ago he cannot organise or retain anything, beyond his weakness
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Wei Zhang is a 74-year-old retired restaurant owner who sustained a hypertensive right thalamic haemorrhage three months ago, presenting with a blood pressure of 214/118 and left hemibody sensory loss and weakness. He was managed conservatively and discharged after twelve days. His son reports that the physical recovery has been steady — he walks with a stick and uses the left hand for gross tasks — but that his father has not resumed any of the organisational roles he held. He ran a restaurant for thirty years and until the haemorrhage still did the family's accounts and negotiated with suppliers; he now cannot follow a two-step request, cannot manage money, and forgets what he has been told unless reminded of the setting. He is slow and says little unprompted, though he understands everything and is not sad. The family emphasise that none of this was present before the haemorrhage. He was poorly adherent to his antihypertensives for years. His father died of an intracerebral haemorrhage at 68. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment.

additional_observations: The haemorrhagic cavity occupies the right thalamus and reaches the posterior limb of the internal capsule, interrupting thalamocortical projections — the anatomy of the dysexecutive and initiation syndrome

Six microbleeds in a strictly deep and infratentorial distribution, with a deep primary haemorrhage: the pattern of hypertensive arteriopathy, and specifically not of cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which requires a strictly lobar distribution
The severe background Fazekas 3 burden with four lacunes indicates that the arteriopathy long predated the haemorrhage
No cortical infarct and no cortical superficial siderosis
mri.impression: Chronic right thalamic haemorrhagic cavity extending to the internal capsule, on a background of severe hypertensive small-vessel arteriopathy: Fazekas 3 white matter change, four lacunes and six strictly deep or infratentorial microbleeds. The distribution is hypertensive rather than amyloid, and the haemorrhage is the final event in a long-standing process.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.query: vascular cognitive impairment diagnostic criteria and secondary prevention

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia after hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage — right thalamic haemorrhage on a background of severe hypertensive small-vessel arteriopathy

differential.key_features: A haemorrhage with multiple microbleeds raises it, and the distinction changes management — but the primary haemorrhage is deep, all six microbleeds are deep or infratentorial, and there is no cortical superficial siderosis, so the Boston criteria are not met and the arteriopathy is hypertensive

The Fazekas 3 burden with four lacunes would support this on its own, and it is part of the picture — but the abrupt onset dated to the haemorrhage and the disproportionate dysexecutive syndrome place the haemorrhagic lesion at the centre
The lesion is haemorrhagic rather than ischaemic and involves the sensory and capsular thalamus; the mechanism is haemorrhage on hypertensive arteriopathy
Abrupt onset dated to the haemorrhage, no premorbid decline reported, cue-responsive recall and preserved hippocampi
Reduced output and initiation with a Geriatric Depression Scale of 4/15 and no reported low mood; this is abulia from capsular-thalamic disconnection

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Cognitive decline dating to a hypertensive thalamic haemorrhage three months earlier, disproportionate to the motor recovery, with no premorbid decline reported by the family

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 19/30 with a dysexecutive profile, reduced initiation and partial cue benefit, dating to the haemorrhage three months earlier

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible contributors excluded; HbA1c 7.8% and LDL 94 mg/dL above target in a patient whose haemorrhage was hypertensive

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Chronic right thalamic haemorrhagic cavity reaching the internal capsule, with Fazekas 3 change, four lacunes and six strictly deep microbleeds — hypertensive arteriopathy, not amyloid angiopathy

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation as the embolic source and for the left ventricular hypertrophy of chronic hypertension
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus rhythm with marked left ventricular hypertrophy and no atrial fibrillation — hypertensive end-organ damage without an embolic source

optimal_actions.action: Image the extracranial carotid arteries to establish whether a large-artery source accounts for the cortical infarcts
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No significant carotid disease, consistent with a haemorrhagic rather than an atherothrombotic substrate

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Dysexecutive syndrome with initiation failure and preserved recognition — thalamocortical disconnection from the haemorrhagic cavity

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Blood-pressure control is the treatment: intensive lowering to a systolic below 130 mmHg with adherence support, since recurrent haemorrhage is the dominant risk in hypertensive arteriopathy; avoid antithrombotic therapy in the absence of a compelling indication given six deep microbleeds and a recent deep haemorrhage; tighten glycaemic and lipid control; and arrange cognitive rehabilitation with family education delivered in the family's language
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Intensive blood-pressure control instituted with adherence support as the intervention that prevents recurrence, antithrombotic therapy withheld in the absence of an indication, and rehabilitation and family education arranged

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Date the cognitive decline against the haemorrhage and confirm the absence of premorbid decline with the family
Distinguish hypertensive from amyloid arteriopathy on the distribution of the haemorrhage and the microbleeds, because the prognosis and the antithrombotic decision differ
Assess cognition in the patient's first language
Obtain MRI with SWI: the microbleed distribution is the diagnostic information
Institute intensive blood-pressure control with adherence support, which is the principal preventive intervention after hypertensive haemorrhage
Withhold antithrombotic therapy where there is no compelling indication after a deep haemorrhage with a heavy microbleed burden
contraindicated_actions: Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy after a deep hypertensive haemorrhage with six microbleeds in the absence of a compelling indication
Do not diagnose cerebral amyloid angiopathy from the presence of microbleeds without applying the distribution rule
Do not accept poor adherence to antihypertensives as a fixed patient characteristic — it is the treatable driver of recurrence
Do not assess cognition through an interpreter-free English or Italian instrument in a first-language Mandarin speaker
Do not treat the abulia as depression by default
key_reasoning_points: Haemorrhagic lesions count toward a vascular dementia diagnosis under VASCOG just as ischaemic ones do, and the temporal criterion applies identically

The distribution rule separates the two arteriopathies: deep haemorrhage with deep and infratentorial microbleeds is hypertensive, while strictly lobar microbleeds with cortical superficial siderosis is amyloid — and the two carry different recurrence risks and antithrombotic implications
A Fazekas 3 burden with four lacunes shows the arteriopathy long predated the haemorrhage, which reframes the haemorrhage as an event within a chronic disease rather than an isolated accident
Blood-pressure control, not an antithrombotic decision, is the intervention that changes outcome after hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage
Adherence is the actionable target in a patient with nineteen years of poorly treated hypertension and a family history of fatal haemorrhage

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which would change the prognosis and prohibit antithrombotic therapy for a different reason
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: All six microbleeds are deep or infratentorial and the primary haemorrhage is thalamic, with no cortical superficial siderosis — this is hypertensive arteriopathy, and the Boston criteria for amyloid angiopathy are not met

red_herrings.intended_effect: Supports a diagnosis of subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia and relegates the haemorrhage to an incidental finding
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The severe burden is real and contributes, but the syndrome began abruptly with the haemorrhage in a patient with no premorbid decline, and the cavity interrupts the thalamocortical projections that explain the dysexecutive picture

key_educational_points: Haemorrhagic lesions satisfy the vascular criteria for dementia in the same way ischaemic ones do
Microbleed and haemorrhage distribution separates hypertensive from amyloid arteriopathy, and the distinction is therapeutic
After deep hypertensive haemorrhage, blood-pressure control is the principal preventive intervention and antithrombotics are avoided without a compelling indication
Cognitive assessment must be conducted in the patient's first language
